facts.fact_text: The applicant notified the Salzburg Federal Police Authority that on All Saints' Day, 1 November 1998, from 9 a.m. until 1 p.m., he would be holding a meeting at the Salzburg municipal cemetery in front of the war memorial.
The purpose of the applicant's planned meeting was to commemorate the Salzburg Jews killed by the SS during the Second World War.
The applicant expected about six participants at the planned meeting.
The participants of the applicant's planned meeting would carry commemorative messages in their hands and attached to their clothes.
The applicant stated that no other means of expression, such as chanting or banners, which might offend piety or undermine public order would be used at the planned meeting.
On 31 October 1998, the Salzburg Federal Police Authority prohibited the applicant's planned meeting.
The Salzburg Federal Police Authority prohibited the applicant's planned meeting on the ground that it would endanger public order and security.
The Salzburg Federal Police Authority ordered that any remedies used against its decision to prohibit the applicant's planned meeting should not have suspensive effect.
As a result of the Salzburg Federal Police Authority's order that remedies should not have suspensive effect, the applicant's planned demonstration could not take place.
On 17 August 1999, the Salzburg Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektion) dismissed an appeal by the applicant against the prohibition of his planned meeting.
On 30 October 1998, the applicant notified the Salzburg Federal Police Authority (Bundespolizeidirektion) under section 2 of the Assembly Act (Versammlungsgesetz) of a planned meeting.
The Salzburg Federal Police Authority relied on section 6 of the Assembly Act (Versammlungsgesetz) when prohibiting the applicant's planned meeting.
The Assembly Act 1953 (Versammlungsgesetz) regulates the exercise of the right to freedom of assembly in Austria.

Section 2(1) of the Assembly Act 1953 (Versammlungsgesetz) provides that any person intending to organise a public assembly or any assembly which is generally open to persons other than invited guests must give the authorities notice in writing at least twenty-four hours in advance.
Section 2(1) of the Assembly Act 1953 (Versammlungsgesetz) requires that the written notice indicate the purpose, place and time of the meeting.
Pursuant to section 6 of the Assembly Act 1953 (Versammlungsgesetz), the competent authority must prohibit any assembly which would contravene criminal law or endanger public order and security.
The Salzburg Federal Police Authority prohibited the applicant's planned meeting on the ground that it would endanger public order and security.

The Salzburg Federal Police Authority found that there was a risk of protests by visitors to the cemetery which could degenerate into open conflict between them and those participating in the applicant's planned assembly.
The Salzburg Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektion) concluded that the prohibition of the applicant's planned assembly was necessary for the maintenance of public order.

The Salzburg Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektion) concluded that the prohibition of the applicant's planned assembly was necessary for the protection of the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) commemoration ceremony.

The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) found that the prohibition of the applicant's assembly was necessary under Article 11 § 2 of the Convention for the protection of the rights and freedoms of others.
